concepts.name: OPEC: Origin, Founding Members, and Mandate
key_dimensions: Founded in 1960 at Baghdad Conference — founding five members: Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Venezuela (NOT UAE or Libya)
Original mandate: coordinate petroleum policies to stabilize oil markets vs. common misconception that it was formed to 'maximize revenue'
Headquartered in Vienna, Austria — trap: often confused with IEA (Paris) or GECF (Doha)
Distinction between founding members and current members — Qatar left in 2019, Ecuador suspended/rejoined/left multiple times

concepts.name: OPEC+ Formation: Genesis and Structural Distinction from OPEC
key_dimensions: OPEC+ formed in 2016 as a response to US shale oil boom and falling oil prices — NOT a formal treaty-based organization
OPEC+ is a loose coalition/alliance, NOT a new organization — OPEC retains its own charter; OPEC+ has no separate headquarters or legal personality
Key non-OPEC members in OPEC+: Russia, Mexico, Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan, Bahrain, Brunei, Malaysia, South Sudan, Sudan — Russia is the most significant
Decision-making trap: OPEC+ decisions require consensus among both OPEC and non-OPEC partners, making enforcement weaker than OPEC alone

concepts.name: OPEC Membership: Current Composition, Exits, and Suspensions
key_dimensions: Current 13 members (as of 2024): Saudi Arabia, Iran, Iraq, UAE, Kuwait, Venezuela, Libya, Nigeria, Gabon, Equatorial Guinea, Congo, Algeria, and Gabon — Indonesia suspended its membership in 2016
Qatar left OPEC in January 2019 citing focus on LNG over oil — significant because Qatar was a founding-era member
Ecuador permanently left in 2020; Indonesia's repeated exits and re-entries are a frequent UPSC trap
Membership criteria trap: OPEC does not require a minimum production threshold — net exporters of crude petroleum are eligible

concepts.name: Production Quota Mechanism: How OPEC+ Sets and Enforces Cuts
key_dimensions: Quotas are voluntary — no binding legal enforcement mechanism exists, making compliance a political rather than legal matter
Baseline production levels (from which cuts are calculated) are often disputed — e.g., Russia and UAE have sought higher baselines
Voluntary Additional Cuts (VACs) vs. collective cuts — Saudi Arabia has often taken unilateral extra cuts beyond the agreed quota
OPEC compliance vs. OPEC+ compliance: non-OPEC members like Russia historically show lower compliance rates — this is a trap in data-based questions

concepts.name: OPEC's Role in Global Oil Price Determination: Market Power and Limits
key_dimensions: OPEC controls ~40% of global oil production and ~80% of proven reserves — but market share has declined due to US shale
OPEC is a cartel under economic theory, but members resist this label — WTO/antitrust law does not apply to sovereign states
Price vs. volume dilemma: cutting production to raise prices can incentivize non-OPEC shale producers to fill the gap — 'shale ceiling' concept
OPEC pricing benchmarks: Brent Crude (North Sea, global benchmark) vs. WTI (US benchmark) vs. Dubai/Oman (Asian benchmark) — OPEC uses Arab Light as its reference basket

concepts.name: India's Strategic Position vis-à-vis OPEC+
key_dimensions: India is the world's third-largest oil importer — heavily dependent on OPEC+ nations (Middle East supplies ~60% of India's crude imports)
India consistently advocates for 'reasonable oil prices' at international forums; PM Modi's direct engagement with Saudi Arabia and UAE on oil pricing
India's response to high prices: diversification to Russia (post-Ukraine war, Russia became India's top supplier in 2022-23 — displacing Saudi Arabia)
India is NOT a member of OPEC or OPEC+; IEA membership: India became an Association Country of IEA in 2017 — not a full member (IEA requires OECD membership as a prerequisite)

concepts.name: OPEC+ and the Russia-Ukraine War: Geopolitical Fault Lines
key_dimensions: Post-2022: OPEC+ refused to significantly increase production despite Western pressure — seen as tacit support for Russia (especially Saudi Arabia's stance)
Russia's discounted oil exports to India and China undermined Western sanctions — OPEC+ framework allowed Russia to maintain export revenues
US-Saudi tension: Biden administration's pressure on Saudi Arabia to increase output was publicly rebuffed — weakening of the 'oil-for-security' petrodollar arrangement
Price cap on Russian oil ($60/barrel by G7) vs. OPEC+ production cuts — these operated simultaneously and in tension

concepts.name: Petrodollar System: Architecture and Its Linkage to OPEC
key_dimensions: 1974 US-Saudi agreement: oil priced exclusively in USD → demand for dollars sustained US monetary hegemony — not a formal treaty, a political arrangement
Petrodollar recycling: OPEC surplus revenues invested in US Treasury bonds → financed US deficits — circular economic dependency
De-dollarization threat: Saudi Arabia's discussions on accepting Yuan for Chinese oil sales (2022-23) — existential challenge to petrodollar
UPSC trap: petrodollar is NOT an official currency — it refers to US dollars earned from petroleum exports

concepts.name: IEA vs. OPEC: Structural Contrast and Mandate
key_dimensions: IEA (International Energy Agency) founded in 1974 as a direct response to the 1973 OPEC oil embargo — consumer-country counterweight to OPEC
IEA membership: OECD countries only (currently 31 members) — India, China, Brazil are NOT members (only Association Countries)
IEA's Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) coordination vs. OPEC's production quota coordination — supply-side vs. demand-side management

Recent convergence: IEA's focus has shifted to clean energy transition (Net Zero by 2050 report) while OPEC defends fossil fuel demand projections — ideological clash relevant for energy diplomacy questions

concepts.name: GECF (Gas Exporting Countries Forum): The 'Gas OPEC' Comparison
key_dimensions: GECF headquartered in Doha, Qatar — founded 2001, intergovernmental organization since 2008
Members include Russia, Iran, Qatar, Algeria, Nigeria — significant overlap with OPEC+ members
GECF does NOT set production quotas — purely a forum for information sharing and policy coordination, unlike OPEC's binding quota mechanism
UPSC trap: GECF is often called 'Gas OPEC' but it lacks OPEC's cartel-like pricing power — natural gas markets are more regionalized (pipeline-dependent) than oil markets

concepts.name: OPEC Fund for International Development (OFID)
key_dimensions: Established in 1976, headquartered in Vienna — provides development finance to non-OPEC, non-OECD developing countries
OFID is a separate legal entity from OPEC — common trap: students assume it is an OPEC subsidiary
Focus areas: energy access, food security, infrastructure — aligns with SDG financing gaps
India has received OFID loans for various infrastructure projects — relevant for India's multilateral financing questions

concepts.name: Saudi Aramco and OPEC's Pricing Architecture: Spare Capacity Doctrine
key_dimensions: Saudi Arabia holds the world's largest oil spare capacity (~2-3 mb/d) — acts as OPEC's 'swing producer' to stabilize prices
Spare capacity concept: deliberate maintenance of unused production ability to respond to market shocks — no other OPEC member has comparable spare capacity
Saudi Arabia as 'price hawk vs. price dove': historically Saudi Arabia has played both roles — favored lower prices in 2014-16 to kill US shale, higher prices post-2020
Saudi Aramco's IPO (2019) and its linkage to Vision 2030: OPEC policy increasingly influenced by Saudi Arabia's fiscal breakeven price (~$70-80/barrel)

concepts.name: OPEC+ Production Cuts of 2020 (COVID-19 Crisis) and the Price War
key_dimensions: March 2020: Russia and Saudi Arabia failed to agree on cuts → Saudi Arabia launched a price war by flooding markets → oil prices crashed to historic lows (WTI futures briefly went negative in April 2020)
April 2020: Largest ever OPEC+ cut agreed — 9.7 million barrels/day — brokered partly with US intervention (Trump administration)
Significance: demonstrated OPEC+'s fragility when major members disagree AND the group's ability to make historic interventions under extreme pressure
Negative oil price event (April 20, 2020): WTI May futures contract settled at -$37/barrel — due to storage constraints, not just demand collapse — frequently misunderstood in exams

concepts.name: Energy Transition and Existential Challenge to OPEC's Relevance
key_dimensions: IEA's Net Zero by 2050 report states no new oil and gas field development needed beyond 2021 — directly challenged by OPEC's demand growth projections
OPEC's World Oil Outlook vs. IEA's World Energy Outlook: two competing narratives on peak oil demand — OPEC projects demand growth till 2045+
Saudi Arabia's Vision 2030 and UAE's diversification: OPEC nations themselves investing in post-oil economies — internal contradiction in defending oil demand
Carbon border taxes (CBAM of EU) and their impact on petrostates' export revenues — links climate policy to OPEC geopolitics

concepts.name: OPEC's 1973 Oil Embargo: Historical Precedent and Lessons
key_dimensions: October 1973: Arab members of OPEC (OAPEC — not all OPEC) embargoed oil to US, Netherlands, and others supporting Israel in Yom Kippur War
OAPEC vs. OPEC trap: the embargo was by OAPEC (Organization of Arab Petroleum Exporting Countries) — a subset of OPEC — non-Arab OPEC members like Venezuela and Iran did not fully participate
Consequences: oil price quadrupled, global stagflation, birth of IEA, accelerated nuclear energy programs in Europe and Japan
Legacy for India: India's vulnerability to oil shocks informed the strategic petroleum reserve policy — India's SPR capacity (~5.33 million tonnes, located in Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru, Padur)

concepts.name: Strategic Petroleum Reserves (SPR): India, US, and IEA Coordination
key_dimensions: IEA mandates member countries to hold 90 days of net import cover as SPR — India is not a member, so not legally bound, but building reserves under IndianStrategic Petroleum Reserves Ltd (ISPRL)
India's SPR locations: Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru, Padur — underground rock cavern storage — Phase 2 expansion to Chandikhol and Padur
US SPR release in 2022 (coordinated with IEA members and India) to counter OPEC+ cuts — India participated as an associate, demonstrating strategic alignment
Trap: SPR is different from commercial storage — SPR can only be released under government authorization for supply emergencies, not for commercial gain

concepts.name: Crude Oil Benchmarks and OPEC Basket Price
key_dimensions: Three major benchmarks: Brent Crude (ICE, London — global benchmark, North Sea), WTI (NYMEX, New York — US benchmark), Dubai/Oman (Asian benchmark, most relevant for India's imports)
OPEC Reference Basket (ORB): weighted average of 13 crude streams from member countries — used to assess revenue impact of quota decisions
Brent-WTI spread: usually Brent > WTI due to transport costs and quality; when reversed, it signals unusual US market conditions
India's import pricing: Indian refiners predominantly use Dubai/Oman benchmark — not Brent — for pricing Middle Eastern crude; relevant for understanding India's import bill calculations

concepts.name: OPEC+ Decision-Making Architecture and the Role of the Joint Ministerial Monitoring Committee (JMMC)
key_dimensions: JMMC established in 2017 to monitor OPEC+ compliance — co-chaired by Saudi Arabia and Russia — meets monthly
OPEC+ has no permanent secretariat or treaty framework — decisions are made at ministerial meetings and implemented voluntarily
Compliance monitoring trap: JMMC can recommend adjustments but cannot penalize non-compliant members — enforcement is entirely reputational/political
Technical Committee vs. Ministerial Level: Technical experts meet to analyze data; Ministers make final decisions — two-tier informal structure

concepts.name: Venezuela and Iran: Sanctions, Exemptions, and OPEC Dynamics
key_dimensions: Iran and Venezuela are subject to US sanctions affecting their oil exports — OPEC+ production baseline calculations often exempt these countries
Iran's nuclear deal (JCPOA) and oil: lifting sanctions could add ~1.5 mb/d to global supply — each negotiation round directly impacts oil price futures
Venezuela's production collapse: from ~3.5 mb/d (2000s) to under 0.7 mb/d (2020s) due to mismanagement and sanctions — OPEC quota became irrelevant for Venezuela
Sanctions exemption trap: Libya and Iran are sometimes exempt from OPEC+ cut agreements due to force majeure (conflict/sanctions) — this is a recurring clause in OPEC+ communiqués

concepts.name: US Shale Revolution and its Disruption of OPEC's Market Power
key_dimensions: Hydraulic fracturing (fracking) made US the world's largest oil producer by 2018 — US produced ~13 mb/d, surpassing Saudi Arabia and Russia
Shale's 'swing producer' role: unlike conventional oil, shale wells can be turned on/off relatively quickly — creates a natural price cap ('shale ceiling') around $50-60/barrel
NOPEC (No Oil Producing and Exporting Cartels Act): US legislation proposed to allow antitrust action against OPEC — never passed but used as diplomatic leverage
OPEC's 2014-16 strategy: Saudi Arabia deliberately kept prices low to bankrupt US shale producers — failed because US shale reduced costs dramatically; this strategy is called 'market share war'
